query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy multilayers, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is controlled by the evolution of local chemical short‐range order (SRO) at the nanoscale interfaces. As the SRO is mechanically degraded under load, its ability to impede dislocation nucleation and motion diminishes, leading to a transformation from a diffusion‐dominated creep regime to one where dislocation-mediated processes (including slip and twinning) govern plastic flow.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating consisting of alternating FCC and BCC high‐entropy alloy layers that initially possess a well‐defined, nominal SRO distribution and severe lattice distortions typical of HEAs.
generation.intervention: Apply a sustained (creep) mechanical load under controlled temperature conditions and introduce a controlled variation in SRO via pre‐annealing treatments versus rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Testing is performed under constant sub‐yield stress at moderate to elevated temperatures that retain the nanoscale multilayer structure and before any catastrophic phase transformation occurs.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical short‐range order (SRO) at the interfaces combined with heterogeneous lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: Initially, regions with strong SRO impede dislocation nucleation and glide, leading to low creep rates. Sustained loading progressively weakens (or destroys) the SRO, thereby reducing the local barriers to dislocation motion. This spatially heterogeneous modification allows dislocations to nucleate and propagate more easily, initiating a switch from diffusion‐controlled deformation to dislocation‐dominated plasticity (including potential contributions from twinning) across the multilayer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under sustained loading, multilayers with a higher initial degree of SRO will exhibit a delayed onset of plastic flow and lower creep strain rates compared to specimens with disrupted SRO. In situ imaging and nanoindentation should reveal that, as loading continues, regions initially resisting deformation (due to strong SRO) gradually succumb, leading to a homogeneous, progressive plastic deformation that correlates with a measurable loss in localized SRO.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy multilayers processed with standard thermal treatments that yield a nominal SRO distribution and characteristic lattice distortion.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply within nanoscale multilayer coatings under stress and temperature regimes that do not trigger bulk phase transformations or catastrophic failure, where interface chemistry and lattice distortion dominate deformation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative influence of SRO relative to other factors (such as grain-boundary contributions or interface mixing) remains uncertain and may vary with slight compositional changes and thermal history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA multilayer samples: one set with enhanced SRO (achieved by controlled annealing) and a second set with intentionally disrupted SRO (achieved by rapid quenching). Subject both sets to identical sustained creep loading while monitoring in situ dislocation dynamics and SRO distribution (using high-resolution TEM or atom-probe tomography).
measurements: Creep strain rate as a function of time
Evolution of dislocation density and distribution
Onset and progression of plastic softening
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets of samples show no statistically significant difference in creep strain rate, dislocation activity, and softening behavior under identical loading conditions, it would falsify the hypothesis that local SRO governs the progressive plastic deformation mechanism in HEA multilayers.

cited_evidence.text: The mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys are receiving continuous attention as they combine excellent strength with ductility,. One of the microscopic origins of their features lies in the slow dislocation activity in these alloys, that is caused by the lattice distortion brought about by the mix of atomic constituents with various sizes. Recently, high-entropy alloys forming single-phase bcc crystals have come into the focus of research. Among them, the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy has become one of the best investigated examples; it is also known as the Senkov alloy. Thus, Xu et al. directly model the shear strength of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy and observe failure by a bcc-to-fcc phase transformation initiating in HfTi rich regions. Liang et al. study how variable fractions of Hf and Ta in HfNbTaTiZr alloys affect the tensile strength. Recently, Hf15Nb40Ta25Ti15Zr15 was found to be both strong and ductile at cryogenic to elevated temperatures. Due to the chemical complexity of these concentrated alloys, the local stoichiometry may deviate from the overall composition leading to local chemical short-range order. Owing to the outstanding softening resistance and thermal stability of BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs), their unique deformation-induced defect structures merit investigation. Therefore, this study evaluated the mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of W-based low- to high-entropy alloys at various temperatures and orientations using nanoindentation and microcompression, complemented by post-mortem TEM and atomistic simulations to observe dislocation populations and their evolution. Results reveal that HEAs exhibit reduced elastic and plastic anisotropy while retaining high-temperature strength. With increasing compositional complexity, planar slip and abrupt stress drops were progressively replaced by homogeneous flow and smoother serrations. Severe lattice distortion promoted dislocation nucleation but impeded long-range glide, enabling cooperative edge and screw dislocation activity that sustained strength and work hardening across temperatures.

Regions with stronger chemical ordering can locally accommodate size differences more efficiently, reducing lattice distortion, whereas regions with weaker or frustrated ordering amplify local strains. This reciprocal interplay governs the heterogeneity of the atomic-scale strain field, providing a fundamental basis for the tunable Hookean and non-Hookean superelasticity observed in the (TiZrHf)50Ni50-xCox alloys. By adjusting the Ni/Co ratio, the balance between chemical ordering and lattice distortion can be finely controlled, resulting in a continuous strain-field landscape that can be precisely tuned through minor compositional variations (<2 at.%), unlike binary or ternary systems where similar adjustments often induce discrete phase transitions. The chemical complexity of the high-entropy system facilitates smooth evolution between strain states, enabling continuous modulation of the elastic response— from Hookean to non-Hookean and back to Hookean—within a single alloy system. Such compositional tuning of elasticity has not been achieved in conventional alloys.
